rv.q: It’s heartening to see these differing experiences of neurodiversity depicted on stage.

But overall this is a muddled, muddied piece of storytelling that feels woefully undercooked, with Theatre Centre’s new artistic director Eleanor Manners failing to find a confident stage language for Stevenson’s skipping script. Luke is the “genius” and Daisy believes herself to be an “idiot”.

My Brother’s a Genius is an eye-opening piece for all ages, providing an insight into life as someone who is neurodiverse in a way we haven’t seen since The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time .
My Brother’s a Genius is an electrifying two-hander that immerses the audience in the siblings’ world through a mix of poetry and grime, capturing the intensity of their experiences.
It’s a powerful piece that helps people like me better understand the neurodivergent world, while also ensuring those within it feel genuinely seen.

cn.t: Critics praise this raw, grime-fueled exploration of neurodivergent twins navigating labels and ambition on a high-rise estate, commending Debris Stevenson's energetic blend of poetry, dance, and music that resonates powerfully with young audiences.
